content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
This paper looks at a multi-agent scenario where they have to communicate, as usual. The question of privacy then arises naturally and this paper provides nice answer to them.

The major concern that I have is that the contributions and techniques used are not that novel and rather well-understood now, So I am not sure that the ICLR community will gain a lot from that paper (with respect to the existing literature).

As a consequence, I am unfortunately not sure that the contributions of this paper are significant enough in its current form to be accepted at ICLR (but I have no doubt it will be accepted elsewhere)
content.justification_for_why_not_higher_score: The techniques are rather classical and well-known. We do not want to see thousands of paper on a privacy variant of this or that problem, with similar tools used, rather new insights and/or techniques and/or models

content.title: Author Response 1
content.comment:
Thank you for your valuable comments and suggestions. We provide our response to each question below.

**Q1. "The motivating example could not provide enough insights for the algorithm."**

We respectfully disagree with this point. Though there exists a difference between the action space of the motivating example and that of the empirical experiments, the algorithm design follows the same intuition strictly. And we show both in the motivating example and in the empirical experiments that this design has its initial success, which makes the intuition and the practise consistent.

**Q2. "The proof of Theorem 5.1 have some minor issue."**

Indeed, the gradient of $f_i^{t-1}$ may depend on $m^{t-1}_i$ and hence $f_i^t$ can depend on the previous message $m^{t-1}_i$. Therefore $f_i^t$ actually may depend on past message functions $f_i^{t-1}$. However, we would like to note that our episode-level privacy guarantee still holds, since Proposition A.1 can still hold when the message function $f_i^t$ at step $t$ depends on previous $t-1$ message functions. Please see Proposition 1 in [1] (or Lemma B.1 in [2]) for details.

**Q3. "However, it seems the author is missing a concurrent work by Liao."**

Thanks for pointing this out and we will also include this paper in our related work section for better literature review.

[1] Mironov, I. (2017, August). Rényi differential privacy. In 2017 IEEE 30th computer security foundations symposium (CSF) (pp. 263-275). IEEE.

[2] Wang, L., Jayaraman, B., Evans, D., \& Gu, Q. (2019). Efficient privacy-preserving stochastic nonconvex optimization. arXiv preprint arXiv:1910.13659.

content.title: Author Response 1
content.comment:
Thank you for your valuable comments and suggestions. We provide our response to each question below.

**Q1. "For example, how does the MARL process look like when agents communicate with each other."**

Yes, each agent sends messages to each other agent before taking action at each time step. As shown in Appendix D, all the communication-based algorithms including DPMAC are allowed to send an $8$-dimensional message at each time step. Also, there is no order of message sending since all the agents send messages to other agents and all the agents receive messages from all other agents simultaneously. We will give the pseudo-codes of our algorithm framework in the future revision of our paper for clarity.

**Q2. "so it's hard to follow why the comparison between Equations (1) and (2) explains the claim that the method alleviates the performance degradation issue."**

Let $\mathcal { N } \left(\mu_i, \Sigma_i\right)$ and $\mathcal{N}\left(\mu_i^{\prime}, \Sigma_i^{\prime}\right)$  be the learned message distribution under privacy constraints and under no privacy constraints respectively. Also, let 
$\mathcal{N}\left(\mu_i^*, \Sigma_i^*\right)$ be the optimal message distribution. The performance degradation issue can be alleviated by learning a message distribution of the sender such that 

$D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(\mathcal { N } \left(\mu_i, \Sigma_i+\sigma_i^2 \mathbf{I}_d\right) \| \mathcal{N}\left(\mu_i^*, \Sigma_i^*\right)\right)$ is not far larger than

$D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(\mathcal{N}\left(\mu_i^{\prime}, \Sigma_i^{\prime}\right) \| \mathcal{N}\left(\mu_i^*, \Sigma_i^*\right)\right)$. More intuitively, we aim to learn a message distribution  $\mathcal { N } \left(\mu_i, \Sigma_i\right)$  under privacy

 constraints, such that the distance between the optimal message sampled from $\mathcal{N}\left(\mu_i^*, \Sigma_i^*\right)$ and the summation of the message sampled from $\mathcal { N } \left(\mu_i, \Sigma_i\right)$  and the Gaussian privacy noise sampled from $\mathcal { N } \left(0, \sigma_i^2 \mathbf{I}_d\right)$ will not be far larger than the distance between the optimal message and the message sampled from the message distribution learned under no privacy constraints $\mathcal{N}\left(\mu_i^{\prime}, \Sigma_i^{\prime}\right)$.

**Q3. "When the authors say the sender are sampled from a learned message distribution, it is also unclear based on what the message distribution is learned. (Maybe this has to do with the lack of clarity about the MARL process.)"**

The message distributions are learned by maximizing the total rewards of the RL agents. Please see Appendix D for the detailed optimization process of the message senders and receivers.

**Q4. "it's a bit hard to think of a scenario where the agents are fully cooperative and care about their privacy at the same time ... but I think autonomous driving is hardly a fully cooperative scenario."**

In general, whether autonomous driving is a fully cooperative scenario or not depends on individual situations. Please see the discussions for when autonomous driving is a fully cooperative scenario in [1,2,3].
There are also other fully cooperative scenarios where protecting the privacy is required.
For example, when multiple hospitals are coordinating with hosting patients, they will need to protect the privacy of their patients at the same time. Similarly, when multiple suppliers are collaborating on a supply chain task, the suppliers might not want to reveal their sensitive information during the communication and coordination.

**Q5. "Minor issue: What is $\mathcal{R}$ in Definition 3.1? In the previous paper, $\mathcal{R}$ is the reward function."**

 $\mathcal{R}$ here is the output space of the function. We would carefully change the notation to avoid the misunderstanding in future revision.

[1] Schmidt, L. M., Brosig, J., Plinge, A., Eskofier, B. M., \& Mutschler, C. (2022). An Introduction to Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning and Review of its Application to Autonomous Mobility. arXiv preprint arXiv:2203.07676.

[2] Althamary, I., Huang, C. W., \& Lin, P. (2019, June). A survey on multi-agent reinforcement learning methods for vehicular networks. In 2019 15th International Wireless Communications \& Mobile Computing Conference (IWCMC) (pp. 1154-1159). IEEE.

[3] Yang, J., Nakhaei, A., Isele, D., Fujimura, K., \& Zha, H. (2018). Cm3: Cooperative multi-goal multi-stage multi-agent reinforcement learning. arXiv preprint arXiv:1809.05188.

content.title: Author Response 1
content.comment:
Thank you for your valuable comments and suggestions. We provide our response to each question below.

**Q1. "I would suggest the authors have more intuitive discussion after the theorem statement."**

We will add more discussions after the theorems in the revision of our paper.

**Q2. "Moreover, it is better to see algorithm framework in the main contents."**

Our algorithm is policy gradient-based and we build it on top of MADDPG. We will clarify this point and give the pseudo-codes of our algorithm framework in the future revision of our paper.

**Q3. "How can we tell from the experimental results that the Nash equilibrium has been achieved?"**

We would like to note that we could consider the task/scenario as a multi-step game, and thus the convergence of multi-agents could indicate the achievement of Nash equilibrium.

**Q4. "Results based on more complex environment can support better the theory."**

We fully agree with the review and we do think that conducting privacy-preserving communication in more realistic environments is an important next step. For example, when multiple hospitals are coordinating with hosting patients, they will need to protect the privacy of their patients at the same time. Similarly, when multiple suppliers are collaborating on a supply chain task, the suppliers might not want to reveal their sensitive information during communication and coordination. The bottleneck for us is that we are not aware of a simulator for such tasks that fully function for our investigation. As such, we plan to leave this extension to future studies.

content.title: Author Response 2
content.comment:
**Q6. "I am confused about this description that in the second line of page 7"**

We would like to note that $m_{(-i)i}=\set{m_{j i}}_{j=1, j \neq i}^N$ has appeared in the equation at the last line of page 6, and each 

$m_{ji}$ is sampled from
 $\mathcal{N}(\mu_j, \Sigma_j+\sigma_j^2 \mathbf{I}_d)$.  Hence  

$\set{\sigma_j}_{j\neq i}$  can serve as a kind of prior knowledge to direct the optimization process of the receiver of agent $i$.  We will revise this part accordingly for better readability.


**Q7. "There exist many unclear descriptions in the experiments section, for example, fig 2b corresponds to $\epsilon=0.1$ instead of $\epsilon=0.01$ as in the paper."**

We would like to note that the statement in the last line in the fifth paragraph on page 9 that "When $\epsilon=0.01$, DPMAC still gains remarkable performance, while other baselines' performance degraded greatly, as shown in Figure 2b." indicates the performance of *baselines* in Figure 2b instead of the performance of *DPMAC with $\epsilon=0.01$* in Figure 2b. Our intention is to show that DPMAC under more stringent privacy constraints may still have better performance than baseline methods. We will revise the statements in this part for better readability.

content.title: Author Response 1
content.comment:
Thank you for your valuable comments and suggestions. We provide our response to each question below.

**Q1. "for example why DPMAC with privacy constraints gains better performance on Predator-Prey than that without privacy constraints? ..."**

In predator-prey we are surprised to see DPMAC with privacy constraints, which means the communication is more stochastic, is better than that without privacy. This might be caused by the task itself, where the predator is chasing the prey and the system dynamic changes rapidly, resulting in the on-time message communication conveying delayed information. We conclude this observation as a special case, and in general the privacy constraints still hurt the communication as shown in other two tasks, and the hurt increases as $\epsilon$ gets smaller. Such observation is consistent for all baselines and DPMAC except one special observation on predator-prey.

**Q2. "It would be better to verify the privacy-preserving property ... have the necessity of privacy-preserving."**

These MPE environments do not require privacy-preserving communication inherently. We choose these environments to conduct the empirical evaluations of privacy-preserving communication since they are the standard environments to evaluate the performance of the deep MARL algorithms in the MARL community.

We fully agree with the review and we do think that conducting privacy-preserving communication in more realistic environments is an important next step. For example, when multiple hospitals are coordinating with hosting patients, they will need to protect the privacy of their patients at the same time. Similarly, when multiple suppliers are collaborating on a supply chain task, the suppliers might not want to reveal their sensitive information during the communication and the coordination. The bottleneck for us is that we are not aware of a simulator for such tasks that fully function for our investigation. As such, we plan to leave this extension to the future study.

**Q3. "I wonder if it is necessary to do experiments on whether real private information (such as personal living routines) can be protected."**

Please see our response to Q2.

**Q4. "The writing of section 5 is hard to understand. There are many notations in section 5.2, but the definition of these seems not complete and not clear. For example, what $m_i$, $p_i$, $u_i$ and $\mu_i$ indicate?"**

We will improve the presentation of Section 5 and provide a table of notations accordingly. Besides,
as stated in the third to the last line on page 5, $p_i$ denotes the message sampled from the learned message distribution,
$\mu_i$ and $\Sigma_i$ are mean vector and the  covariance matrix of learned message distribution of sender respectively. 
Also, as stated in fourth line on page 6, $u_i$ is the privacy noise, and $m_i=p_i+u_i$ is the privatized messages to be sent.

**Q5. "What’s the relationship between equations (1) and (2)..."**

Yes, Equation (1) is the learning objective of the message sender under no privacy constraints, and Equation (2) is the learning objective of the message sender under privacy constraints. Also, we would like to note that the inequality about KL divergence in the third line under Equation (2) is not guaranteed to hold. Whether it holds depends on the specific optimization process of the message sender's neural networks, and we said that ``it is possible ... such that 
$D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(\mathcal { N } \left(\mu_i, \Sigma_i+\sigma_i^2 \mathbf{I}_d\right) \| \mathcal{N}\left(\mu_i^*, \Sigma_i^*\right)\right) \leq $

$D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(\mathcal{N}\left(\mu_i^{\prime}, \Sigma_i^{\prime}\right) \| \mathcal{N}\left(\mu_i^*, \Sigma_i^*\right)\right)$
". However, from the experimental results, this inequality indeed holds in the learning process on the predator-prey environment due to that  DPMAC with $\epsilon=0.10$ and $\epsilon=1.00$ has better performance than DPMAC under no privacy constraints.

 Furthermore, though this inequality does not hold on the cooperative navigation (CN) and cooperative communication and navigation (CCN) environments, it is also reasonable to believe that 
$D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(\mathcal { N } \left(\mu_i, \Sigma_i+\sigma_i^2 \mathbf{I}_d\right) \| \mathcal{N}\left(\mu_i^*, \Sigma_i^*\right)\right)$ 
is not far larger than 

$D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(\mathcal{N}\left(\mu_i^{\prime}, \Sigma_i^{\prime}\right) \| \mathcal{N}\left(\mu_i^*, \Sigma_i^*\right)\right)$ since the performance of DPMAC under privacy constraints does not have a serious performance degeneration,  compared with the performance of DPMAC under no privacy constraints.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper addresses the private-preserving problem in multi-agent cooperative communication. It proposes a differentially private multi-agent communication (DPMAC) algorithm, which protects the sensitive information of individual agents by adding noise when sending messages to others with rigorous $(ε, δ)$-differential privacy (DP) guarantee. Each agent is equipped with a sender that sends its partial observation disturbed by stochastic noise, and a receiver integrates all other agents’ messages. It proves the existence of the Nash equilibrium for cooperative games with privacy-preserving communication. Experiments on the MPE show that DPMAC clearly outperforms other algorithms in privacy-preserving scenarios and gains competitive performance in non-private scenarios.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
1. This paper is the first attempt to develop a MARL private communication framework, with a theoretical analysis on the private guarantee.
2. Experiments on MEP show proposed DPMAC gains comparable performance under non-private settings and better performance than other privatized baselines under private setting.
 
Weaknesses:
1. However, explanations of experiment results are lacking, for example why DPMAC with privacy constraints gains better performance on Predator-Prey than that without privacy constraints? What is the main conclusion on the ablation study of hyperparameters \epsilon? The results on three environments seem not consistent, the hyperparameter \epsilon has a significant impact only on predator-prey when training steps up to 1e6.
2. It would be better to verify the privacy-preserving property in a more rational scenario that naturally possesses private requirements; agents in an MPE environment seem not to have the necessity of privacy-preserving.
3. I wonder if it is necessary to do experiments on whether real private information (such as personal living routines) can be protected.
4. Why the Nash existence is important in a cooperative game, the Nash does not always correspond to the solution with the greatest payoff in a cooperative game. And the first two lines in section 6 clarify that the “Many cooperative multi-agent games enjoy the existence of a unique NE”, but this paper proves the existence of NE instead of unique NE. It would be better to unify these statements.
5.The theoretical analysis on Nash existence is given, but it would be better to conduct experiments about NE existence for completeness.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity:
* The writing of section 5 is hard to understand. There are many notations in section 5.2, but the definition of these seems not complete and not clear. For example, what $m_i,p_i,u_i$, and $\mu_i$ indicate?
* What’s the relationship between equations (1) and (2), (1) hope to learn an unconstrained message sender, (1) hope to learn a constrained message sender, right? And why the inequality about KL- divergence holds in the third line under eq. (2)?
* I am confused about this description that in the second line of page 7, “utilize the prior knowledge $\sigma_i$ ”, the  $\sigma_i$ seems not defined as “prior knowledge” hereinbefore， it is defined as Gaussian noise, and it has not appeared in the equation at the last line of page 6.
* There exist many unclear descriptions in the experiments section, for example, fig 2b corresponds to $\epsilon=0.1$ instead of $\epsilon=0.01$ as in the paper.

Quality: Theoretical analysis is sufficient on privacy guarantee and Nash existence, but the experiments especially the explanation of the results are lacking.

Novelty: This paper firstly proposes the problem of private-preserving communication in cooperative MARL. It is original, however, the experiments are not conducted in environments with private-preserving requirements, thus I am concerned about the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm on privacy protection.

Reproducibility: The overall structure of the message sender and receiver is in the form of equations, but the detailed setting of the sender under privacy and non-privacy constraints is not clear to me. It would be clearer to give a pseudocode of the framework.
content.summary_of_the_review: This work firstly proposes the private-preserving problem in multi-agent cooperative communication, it is original. Theoretical analysis is sufficient on privacy guarantee and Nash's existence. However, experiments are weak and do not prove the algorithm can protect the privacy.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a novel differentially private communication algorithm for cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning. Specifically, the authors proposed the differentially private multi-agent communication (DPMAC). The proposed algorithm protects the sensitive information of individual agents by equipping each agent with a local message sender with rigorous differential privacy guarantee. To achieve this, a stochastic message sender for each agent respectively with DP requirement into the sender. This can automatically adjusts the learned message distribution to alleviate the instability caused by DP noise. They also theoretically proved that the existence of a Nash equilibrium in cooperative MARL with privacy-preserving communication. To validate the proposed algorithm, the authors leveraged a decentralized navigation communication environment to show the superiority over the baseline methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: 

This paper develops a novel algorithm for MARL to cope with differential privacy in individual agents. The authors design new mechanism, privacy-preserving local sender and privacy-aware receiver. The mechanism looks technically sound to protect sensitive information for agents. The authors also theoretically prove the differential privacy guarantees and analyze two scenarios of games to show the Nash equilibrium. The experimental results are also promising to demonstrate the outperforming capability, though the environment is simple. Overall, the paper is well written and easy to follow.

Weaknesses:

Typically, MARL suffers from high computation and communication overhead. This work fails to show the complexities, which is a weakness. Particularly, to handle DP issue, it would be great to see how those complexities are affected for the proposed DPMAC framework. Additionally, the analysis for the equilibrium analysis seems not sufficient. I would suggest the authors have more intuitive discussion after the theorem statement. 

Moreover, it is better to see algorithm framework in the main contents. Based on the current work, it is not clear what exactly underlying algorithm is. Is it Q-learning based or policy gradient-based? As MARL covers a large spectrum of different algorithm, such as the MADDPG in the comparison. Or DPMAC can be used with any centralized counterpart?

How can we tell from the experimental results that the Nash equilibrium has been achieved?

Though the experimental results look convincing, the environment is way too simple. Results based on more complex environment can support better the theory.

*************************Post-rebuttal*************************
I appreciate the responses from the authors. After carefully reviewing the rebuttal, I would just keep my current score.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The clarity and quality of this paper are good. The theoretical novelty also seems decent. While the empirical evidences may require some more work to validate the theory.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper presents a novel differentially private communication algorithm for cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning. The authors develop a privacy-preserving local sender and privacy-aware receiver for individual agents. They also mathematically analyze the privacy guarantee and the equilibrium analysis. The experimental results look promising to outperform the baseline methods, but they are based on a simple environment. Overall I think the draft looks technically sound and solid, but some additional work are required to clarify and validate the theory.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper studies communication in multiagent reinforcement learning that preserves privacy. It adopts the concept of differential privacy to approach the problem and proposes an algorithm that is able to protect individual agents' information privacy. The authors also use a stochastic message sender for each agent to address the instability issue. The authors also prove the existence of a Nash equilibrium in the cooperative multiagent reinforcement learning model. Theoretical results are evaluated empirically.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

The idea of considering differential privacy in MARL setting is interesting and novel.

Weakness:

Some parts of the paper is not clear. For example, how does the MARL process look like when agents communicate with each other. Do they send messages to every other agent at every time step before they take an action? How many messages can be sent by each of them in a time step? What is the sequence of the messages and the order of message sending? 

The methods described in Section 5.1 also seem to lack some necessary details, so it's hard to follow why the comparison between Equations (1) and (2) explains the claim that the method alleviates the performance degradation issue.  When the authors say the sender are sampled from a learned message distribution, it is also unclear based on what the message distribution is learned. (Maybe this has to do with the lack of clarity about the MARL process.)

In addition to the clarity issue, it's a bit hard to think of a scenario where the agents are fully cooperative and care about their privacy at the same time. The authors mentioned autonomous driving, but I think autonomous driving is hardly a fully cooperative scenario (where agents share exactly the same reward function). 

Minor issue: What is $\mathcal{R}$ in Definition 3.1? In the previous paper, $\mathcal{R}$ is the reward function.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: I find the paper very clear at some parts but hard to follow at others. The key idea and the approach proposed look novel.
content.summary_of_the_review: In summary, a paper motivated by an interesting idea but lacking clarity at some parts as well as convincing motivating applications.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This work focused on multi-agent reinforcement learning with a privacy guarantee. The author first shows that a privacy-aware receiver could 
alleviate the instability caused by random Gaussian noise. Based on this idea, the author proposes the differentially private multi-agent communication (DPMAC) framework and proves the existence of the Nash equilibrium. In addition, the result of the experiments shows that
DPMAC outperforms other algorithms in privacy-preserving scenarios and gains competitive performance in non-private scenarios.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

The author provided the first analyses on multi-agent reinforcement learning with a privacy guarantee and proposed a novel framework (DPMAC). In addition, both the theoretical results and the experiments show that the proposed algorithm is efficient and can provide a differential privacy guarantee.

Weakness:

1. The motivating example could not provide enough insights for the algorithm. In this example, the bit $b_i$ should be generated from {0,1} rather $[0,1]$. Though this example shows that a privacy-aware receiver could alleviate the instability caused by random Gaussian noise, it seems difficult to extend the result to a continuous situation and can only provide limited insights for the framework.

2. The proof of Theorem 5.1 have some minor issue. In detail, the differential privacy guarantee is based on Lemma A.1 and Propositional A.1, which require the function $f_i$ to be fixed. However, the DPMAC algorithm's parameter $\theta_i$ is optimized with the gradient method. Thus, the function $f_i$ may be related to the message, and in this situation, previous analyses cannot provide a guarantee for differential privacy.

3. For the related work, the author mentions Zhou (2022) subsequently takes the first step to establish the sublinear regret in linear mixture Markov decision processes (MDPs). However, it seems the author is missing a concurrent work by Liao(2022), which also provided a differential guarantee in linear mixture MDP and was posted on arXiv 1.5 months before Zhou (2022).

Liao C, He J, Gu Q. Locally differentially private reinforcement learning for linear mixture markov decision processes

content.title: DPMAC: Differentially Private Communication for Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
keywords: Communication in deep multi-agent reinforcement learning
content.TL;DR: We make the first attempt to develop a privacy-preserving communication framework for MARL, named \textit{DPMAC}.
content.abstract: Communication lays the foundation for cooperation in human society and in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL). Humans also desire to maintain their privacy when communicating with others, yet such privacy concern has not been considered in existing works in MARL. We propose the \textit{differentially private multi-agent communication} (DPMAC) algorithm, which protects the sensitive information of individual agents by equipping each agent with a local message sender with rigorous $(\epsilon, \delta)$-differential privacy (DP) guarantee. In contrast to directly perturbing the messages with predefined DP noise as commonly done in privacy-preserving scenarios, we adopt a stochastic message sender for each agent respectively and incorporate the DP requirement into the sender, which automatically adjusts the learned message distribution to alleviate the instability caused by DP noise. Further, we prove the existence of a Nash equilibrium in cooperative MARL with privacy-preserving communication, which suggests that this problem is game-theoretically learnable. Extensive experiments demonstrate a clear advantage of DPMAC over baseline methods in privacy-preserving scenarios.
